content: The data provided outlines various aspects of blood donation, blood component preparation, and laboratory screening for transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs) across different countries and years. Below is a professional interpretation of the key points: 1. Platelet and Granulocyte Apheresis Donations: A total of 132,275 platelet apheresis donations were recorded, alongside 14 granulocyte apheresis donations. Plasma apheresis donations amounting to 139 liters were excluded from this count. 2. Blood Donation Data by Country: In the United Republic of Tanzania, no apheresis donations were reported from 2011 to 2013. In the United States, apheresis donations were consistently reported, with 1,978,000 in 2011, 1,100,424 in 2012, and 1,027,325 in 2013. These included donations from first-time and repeat voluntary non-remunerated donors (VNRDs), family/replacement donors, and paid donors. Uruguay reported 408 apheresis donations in 2012 and 112 in 2013. Vietnam reported 492 apheresis donations in 2011, 535 in 2012, and 470 in 2013, with contributions from both first-time and repeat VNRDs. Zimbabwe reported 160 apheresis donations in 2011, 107 in 2012, and 15 in 2013. 3. Laboratory Screening for TTIs: Screening for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis was mandatory in most countries. Some countries also screened for Chagas disease, malaria, and HTLV I/II. For example, Afghanistan required screening for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis for all donations. Algeria and Angola also mandated screening for these infections, with additional testing for malaria in Angola. In some countries, such as Andorra and Azerbaijan, no data on laboratory screening were reported. 4. Blood Centers Performing Laboratory Screening: The number of blood centers performing laboratory screening for TTIs varied by country. For instance, in 2013, Afghanistan had 14 centers, Algeria had 200, and Angola had 139 centers. Participation in external quality assessment schemes (EQAS) for TTI testing was limited in some countries. For example, Afghanistan reported no participation in EQAS from 2011 to 2013, while Algeria had no data available for 2012 and 2013. 5. Blood Component Preparation: Blood component preparation was reported in several countries, with varying levels of separation of whole blood donations into components such as red cells, plasma, and platelets. For example, in 2013, Germany reported 70 blood centers preparing components, with 100% of whole blood donations separated into components. In Uganda, 7 centers prepared components, with 60% of whole blood donations separated. Some countries, such as Benin, used centrifugation for component preparation, while others relied on sedimentation methods. 6. Screening and Testing Practices: In some countries, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, testing for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis was centralized, with samples sent to national or regional centers for retesting. In Japan, all nine screening laboratories of the Japanese Red Cross participated in national EQAS for NAT screening of HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. However, there was no EQAS for serological tests. 7. Proportion of Donations Screened for TTIs: In countries like France, Gabon, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, 100% of donations were screened for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis from 2011 to 2013. Selective testing for Chagas disease was performed in some countries, such as Gabon, where only donors at risk were screened. 8. Blood Component Data: The preparation of blood components varied significantly. For instance, in 2013, Germany prepared 743,222 units of blood components, while Uganda prepared 121,761 units. Some countries, such as Finland, exclusively used solvent-detergent-treated fresh frozen plasma (FFP). 9. Challenges and Limitations: Data gaps were evident in several countries, with some not reporting laboratory screening or blood component preparation data. In some cases, only partial data were available, or estimations were made due to missing reports from major centers.
